name: TX-30
label: Safe D

key_factors: District's post-redistricting partisan lean of D+25
Haynes' overwhelming fundraising edge (about $657K to $17K) plus outside support
Prediction markets price the Democratic nominee near 97%
No public polls or expert ratings, so fundamentals drive the call
model.rationale: The open Dallas-area seat's D+25 partisan lean, Haynes' roughly 38-to-1 fundraising advantage, and prediction markets pricing the Democrat at about 97% all point the same direction. With no polls or expert ratings available, the strong fundamentals make the outcome's direction clear even if the exact margin is uncertain.
model.watch: A late infusion of outside spending for Jackson or unusually depressed turnout in a low-salience open-seat race could narrow the margin, though flipping the outcome would require a historic partisan shift.
notes: No expert rater lists this race; fundamentals point clearly one way (post-redistricting), so it is treated as safe for that party.
No usable general-election polls; forecast rests on fundamentals and expert ratings.

overview:
Texas's 30th District, centered on Dallas, remains firmly Democratic after redistricting, with a partisan lean of about 25 points. The seat is open this year, and Democrats nominated Frederick Haynes III, a pastor who has raised roughly $657,000, holds about $200,000 on hand, and benefits from about $200,000 in outside support. Republican Everett Jackson has raised about $17,000 with roughly $1,200 remaining, leaving minimal resources for a competitive campaign.

No public general-election polls cover the race, and no expert raters have weighed in. Prediction markets price the Democratic nominee at about a 97 percent chance of winning. The combination of the district's strong partisan tilt, the large fundraising gap, and market pricing points to a comfortable Democratic win, with the main uncertainty limited to the size of the margin rather than the outcome.
